presentingComplaint: Six weeks of low-grade evening fever, profound loss of appetite and 8 kg weight loss in a frail nursing-home resident, with recent-onset confusion.
history: A 78-year-old frail widower resident of an old-age home was brought in by staff for 6 weeks of insidious ill-health rather than any dramatic illness. Instead of the classic high spiking fevers, he has had only low-grade evening temperatures, drenching night sweats twice weekly, and relentless anorexia with an 8 kg unintentional weight loss. Family attributed his fatigue and increasing daytime drowsiness to 'old age' and early dementia. There is a mild dry cough but no significant sputum, haemoptysis or pleuritic pain. He was treated for smear-positive pulmonary TB 40 years ago and 'completed' therapy. He is not diabetic and not HIV-tested. Background: age-related frailty, mild chronic kidney disease and a poor nutritional state (BMI 17). No recent travel. Over the last week home staff noted he had become apathetic and intermittently disoriented, prompting review. This cryptic, wasting, low-grade febrile illness in a frail elderly host - with pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly rather than a florid pulmonary picture - is the classic 'cryptic disseminated TB' of the aged.
examination: Cachectic, frail elderly man, apathetic but rousable. Pallor present. No lymphadenopathy palpable. Chest: scattered fine bibasal crepitations, no focal consolidation. Abdomen: soft, non-tender, with a firm hepatomegaly 3 cm and splenomegaly 2 cm below costal margins. No ascites, no jaundice. Dilated fundoscopy by ophthalmology revealed bilateral choroidal tubercles (pale yellow retinal lesions) - a near-pathognomonic sign. Mild global slowing of cognition; no neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit.
imaging: Chest radiograph: innumerable uniform 1-3 mm nodules distributed evenly throughout both lung fields - a classic miliary pattern (though initially reported as 'age-related changes' on portable film). High-resolution CT chest: diffuse randomly distributed micronodules confirming miliary spread; mild hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal imaging. No large cavity.
microbiology: Sputum Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra: MTB detected, rifampicin resistance not detected. Sputum AFB smear scanty positive. Blood cultures for pyogenic organisms sterile. Bone marrow aspirate/trephine: caseating granulomata with AFB, consistent with marrow involvement explaining pancytopenia. Urine and mycobacterial blood culture sent.
differentialDiagnoses: Disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis - cryptic form in the frail elderly (confirmed)
Disseminated malignancy / lymphoma with B-symptoms and marrow infiltration
Pyrexia of unknown origin under evaluation
finalDiagnosis: Disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis presenting cryptically in a frail 78-year-old - reactivation with haematogenous dissemination, marrow and hepatic involvement, choroidal tubercles, and probable early CNS/SIADH involvement.
citations: WHO - Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis: Treatment of Drug-Susceptible TB - 2022
ICMR/NTEP (India) - Guidelines for Programmatic Management of Tuberculosis - 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Tuberculosis (Miliary/Disseminated TB)
stewardship: Anti-tuberculous therapy, not broad-spectrum antibacterials. Start standard 4-drug intensive phase: isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol (HRZE), with pyridoxine, weight-based dosing and hepatic/renal monitoring given frailty, CKD and hypoalbuminaemia. Screen for and manage early meningeal involvement; add corticosteroid only if TB meningitis/pericarditis confirmed. Avoid empiric broad-spectrum antibacterials - this is a targeted, notifiable-disease treatment.
contraindications: Reduce/adjust ethambutol and pyrazinamide dosing for CKD (eGFR-based); monitor for ethambutol optic toxicity given baseline visual/retinal disease
High risk of drug-induced hepatotoxicity in frail, hypoalbuminaemic elderly - baseline and serial LFTs mandatory
Avoid concurrent nephrotoxic and QT-prolonging agents; watch rifampicin drug interactions with any polypharmacy
edgeCases: Portable chest films frequently miss the miliary pattern in the elderly - a normal or 'age-related' film does not exclude disseminated TB
Cryptic miliary TB can present as PUO or as unexplained pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly, mimicking haematological malignancy
Hyponatraemia (SIADH) and subtle confusion should prompt evaluation for coexisting TB meningitis (LP)
Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy are near-pathognomonic and allow rapid bedside diagnosis
expectedMaiK: In a frail elderly patient, a cryptic wasting febrile illness with weight loss, night sweats, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly and a miliary chest pattern is disseminated TB until proven otherwise; confirm with Xpert MTB/RIF and start weight-adjusted HRZE.
expectedNextQuestions: Any prior TB treatment, TB contact, or incomplete past therapy?
Is there headache, confusion or neck stiffness suggesting meningeal spread (indication for LP)?
HIV status, diabetes, steroid/immunosuppressant use or other immunocompromise?
Duration and pattern of fever, night sweats and quantified weight loss?
